report.source_text: Currently, 20 months after the surgery, the patient feels good and does not report any alarming symptoms. Measurements of arterial tension and the heart rate carried out at home show normal results. Follow-up abdominal and thyroid ultrasonography is normal; isotopic analysis performed 8 months after the surgery (131- I MIBG scintigraphy) did not reveal any regions of abnormal accumulation of the tracer. The level of catecholamines and methoxycatecholamines in the control 24-h urine collection was normal (Table 1). Ophthalmic examinations showed significant regression of the changes described earlier. The patient’s vision has improved substantially and there are no signs of scotoma. Follow-up MRI of the CNS did not reveal abnormalities besides the presence of the arachnoid cyst. The lesions detected previously may have resulted from the developing encephalopathy. Slight muscular hyperthrophy of the left ventricle persists.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome with bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 14-year-old boy with uncomplicated perinatal history presented with bilateral scotoma, periodic headaches, and dizziness. Ophthalmologic examination revealed increased intraocular pressure and hypertensive retinopathy. Physical examination documented severe arterial hypertension (180/135 mmHg). Contrast CT of the head showed arachnoid cysts and multiple brain foci. Detailed history elicited periodic anxiety attacks accompanied by skin pallor and excessive sweating (E007)—classic catecholamine-release symptoms. Biochemical testing (E008) demonstrated markedly elevated serum noradrenaline with normal adrenaline and substantially elevated 24-hour urine catecholamines and metanephrines, confirming catecholamine excess. Abdominal CT imaging (E009) localized bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas: right adrenal lesion 50×40×52 mm and left adrenal lesion 24 mm in diameter. Genetic testing (E013) identified a VHL ex.1 p.Y112C mutation, confirming von Hippel-Lindau syndrome as the underlying diagnosis. Surgical intervention was performed. At 20-month follow-up (E014), the patient demonstrated excellent clinical response with normalized blood pressure, normal catecholamine levels on repeat 24-hour urine collection, significant regression of retinopathy with resolution of scotoma and improved vision, normal follow-up abdominal and thyroid ultrasonography, normal 131-I MIBG scintigraphy at 8 months post-surgery, and normal follow-up CNS MRI except for the persistent arachnoid cyst. Slight left ventricular hypertrophy persisted.
